item.title: Collaborative Editing
item.description: In this tutorial, you and a teammate work on the same design at the same time. You save a design, share it, watch your teammate join as a live collaborator, edit together, and run a short review in a comment thread. Along the way you learn the four separate mechanisms behind collaboration in Kanvas: the live session, access, comments, and saving. Each one explains a different part of what you see.

item.title: Share a Design Across Organizations
item.description: In this tutorial, an Organization Admin at one company asks an engineer at another company to review a private design. By the end, you will have given someone outside your organization access to one design, held a review in a comment thread, and removed that access. Along the way, you will learn what a grant gives someone, where Kanvas checks permissions, and why the review itself has to happen in comments.

item.title: Build a GCP Data Pipeline Design
item.description: In this tutorial you follow Zara Osei, Team Admin of the Orbital Labs Infrastructure Team, as she models the team’s Google Cloud data pipeline in Kanvas. The pipeline ingests events through Pub/Sub, processes them with Dataflow, writes analytical results to BigQuery, archives raw payloads to Cloud Storage, and runs alongside a GKE cluster. The result is a design named data-pipeline-gcp: a reviewable, shareable model of the architecture that lives in the team’s workspace instead of in a slide deck.

item.title: Deploy AWS EC2 Instances
item.description: In this tutorial you create a VPC network and EC2 instances in your AWS account without leaving Kanvas. You deploy three designs from the catalog, in order, to your own Kubernetes cluster: a controller that talks to AWS, a VPC network, and the EC2 instances that run inside it. Each AWS resource is a Kubernetes custom resource in the design, and a controller in the cluster turns that resource into real infrastructure.

item.title: Deploy Azure Resources
item.description:
In this tutorial you install Azure Service Operator (ASO) in your own Kubernetes cluster, then design an Azure resource group and a storage account inside it, deploy both from Kanvas, and find them in the Azure portal. You manage real Azure infrastructure with the same design, validate, and deploy loop you use for Kubernetes workloads, and the cluster keeps that infrastructure matched to the design.

The trade-off is indirection. Kanvas never calls Azure. It applies Kubernetes objects to your cluster, and ASO turns those objects into Azure resources in the background. A successful deploy means the cluster accepted the objects; the Azure resources follow a little later, and Azure-side failures surface on the objects in the cluster, not in the deploy summary.
